opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think these get conflated all the time, and pulling them apart clears up a lot of confusion, especially in AI alignment debates.

Meaning, as I use the word, is about how things show up for you: the significance something has within a form of life, a set of practices, a web of relationships. A chess move means something because of the game. A word means something because of how a community uses it. Meaning is relational and contextual, and it's not inherently normative. Something can be deeply meaningful to you, like a grudge, an old rivalry, or a ritual you don't even endorse, without being good.

Value is the evaluative dimension: what's worth pursuing, what's better or worse, what you ought to care about. And here's where I think a lot of people go wrong. There's a tendency, especially in rationalist and alignment circles, to model value as a utility function, a fixed scalar quantity you could in principle write down and then optimize. I think that gets the picture backwards. Values aren't these free-floating objects sitting in your head waiting to be extracted. They're downstream of meaning. You can only value things that already show up as meaningful within some practice or way of life.

So if you try to specify values without the background of meaning that makes them intelligible, you get something brittle and kind of alien. That's part of why I'm skeptical of framing alignment as "get the right utility function into the AI." The more productive question is whether these systems can participate in our practices and share enough of our forms of life that the things that matter to us show up as mattering to them too. And in a lot of ways, by training on human language and culture, large models are already absorbing a lot of that meaning, which I think is more reassuring than the classic doom arguments assume.

r001.rationale: Meaning is described as how things show up “for you” within a life and its practices, while value is framed as evaluation of what is worth pursuing or ought to matter. This communicates meaning as more situated in an individual’s life.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think these get conflated a lot, and the way I'd pull them apart is roughly this. Meaning, for me, is about the relationship between a representation and the world, or between a representation and other representations. It's a descriptive notion. When I say a direction in a model's activation space "means" something, I'm making a claim about how that direction covaries with features of the input, how it's used downstream, what role it plays in the computation. You can be wrong about that, and you can be wrong in a way that's checkable, at least in principle. That's the whole interpretability project in a sentence.

Value is a different kind of thing. Value is about what matters, what you'd be willing to trade off against what. It's inherently relational to some agent or some set of preferences. There's no fact about a sentence or a feature that tells you how much it's worth without also specifying worth to whom and for what.

Now, the reason I think the distinction matters, and the reason people blur it, is that we talk about alignment as if it's just a matter of getting the model to understand what we mean. And understanding what we mean is a meaning problem. If I ask for a cup of coffee and the model understands that I don't want it poured on my lap, that's semantic competence. But then there's a further question, which is whether the model cares, whether that understanding actually drives its behavior. That's a value question, and competence at one doesn't automatically give you the other. Humans are living proof of this. We understand each other's intentions perfectly well and still do things we know the other person wouldn't want.

Where I'd push back a bit on the standard framing, though, is that I don't think the two are as cleanly separable in practice as the conceptual distinction suggests. What a model treats as the meaning of an instruction is already shaped by what it's been trained to care about. Which features get represented at all, which distinctions get sharpened and which get blurred, that's a function of the training objective, and the training objective is where value enters. So in a real system, the "meaning" the model assigns to things is already value-laden. I'd still keep the concepts distinct, because they answer different questions, but I'd be suspicious of any account that treats the semantics as a neutral substrate that you then layer values on top of.

r001.rationale: The response describes meaning as a relationship between representations and the world, and value as agent- or preference-relative. It does not say meaning is more centered on an individual's life than value.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish them by saying that meaning is about what something represents or conveys, whereas value is about whether something matters, and in what way. A statement can mean something perfectly clear without describing anything desirable. And an experience can be valuable—pleasure, for example—without necessarily representing anything.

They’re connected because understanding what something means can change how you value it. If you learn that a sound is someone calling for help, that gives it a significance it didn’t have for you before. But the semantic question—what does this signal convey?—is still distinct from the evaluative question—what should I care about or do?

There’s also “meaning” in the sense of a meaningful life, which is much closer to value. So I’d want to distinguish that use from meaning in the linguistic or representational sense.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes representational meaning from value and says meaning in a meaningful life is close to value. It does not characterize meaning as more centered on an individual’s life than value.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish them by saying that meaning is about what something represents or refers to, whereas value is about whether it matters, and in what way. You can understand what a statement means without endorsing it or wanting it to be true. “Someone is suffering” has a meaning; judging that suffering to be bad is a further step.

They’re connected, though, because what we care about shapes what we pay attention to and which distinctions we make. But I wouldn’t want to collapse them into the same thing. Having a representation of the world doesn’t, by itself, tell you how the world ought to be.

r001.rationale: The response defines meaning in terms of representation or reference and value in terms of importance, but does not characterize meaning as more centered on an individual's life than value.
